title: Lazarus, come out (John 11:1–44)
hook: Jesus weeps at his friend's tomb, then calls him out

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zacchaeus up a sycamore, called down by name. Your line was he knows your name. What did you make right? Today, a friend's name called into a tomb. Day sixty.

Think of the phone call nobody wants. Someone you love is sick, and you're far away, and you have to decide how fast to come. Now go to Bethany, a village just outside Jerusalem. Two sisters, Martha and Mary, send word to Jesus about their brother Lazarus. Their words, in the King James Bible, are simple: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Not our brother. The one you love. They were close friends. And John says something puzzling: Jesus loved them, and so he stayed where he was two more days. By the time he arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Today's word: Lazarus.
screen: `THE PHONE CALL NOBODY WANTS.` → `HE WHOM THOU LOVEST IS SICK.` → `FOUR DAYS IN THE TOMB.`

segments.voice: Martha hears he's coming and runs out to meet him on the road, and she's honest: if you had been here, my brother wouldn't have died. And he tells her: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Then Mary comes, and she falls at his feet and says the very same words: if you had been here. She's weeping, and everyone with her is weeping. And John says he was deeply moved and troubled. He asks, where have you laid him? They say, come and see. And then the shortest verse in the English Bible, two words: "Jesus wept." Think about that. He knows what he's about to do. He's about to call Lazarus out. And he still weeps. He doesn't skip past the grief to the happy ending. He stands in it with his friends. The people watching say: "Behold how he loved him!" At the tomb he says, take away the stone, and practical Martha objects, in the King James words: "Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days." They roll it away anyway. He prays aloud, then shouts: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man walks out, still wrapped hand and foot in grave clothes, his face bound with a cloth. And the last line is almost tender in its plainness: "Loose him, and let him go." Somebody has to unwrap him. In John's Gospel this is the last and greatest sign before the cross, and it's the one that makes the authorities decide he must die. The name Lazarus comes from the Hebrew Eleazar: God has helped.
screen: `IF THOU HADST BEEN HERE.` · `I AM THE RESURRECTION.` · `TWO WORDS: JESUS WEPT.` · `LOOSE HIM, AND LET HIM GO.` · then, large: `LAZARUS, COME FORTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Is there one thing you haven't let yourself cry about? A loss, a disappointment, a door that closed, a person who's gone. Something you moved past too quickly because there was too much to do. Let it come to mind. You don't have to force tears. Just stop holding it back. If tears come, let them. Jesus wept at a tomb he was about to open. Grief isn't a lack of faith. If you pray, you can bring the grief as it is. The bell holds the time.
Lazarus. From the Hebrew Eleazar, God has helped. A friend four days in the tomb, wept over, and called out by name.
Your line: jesus wept. Today, let yourself feel one grief instead of rushing past it, and if someone near you is grieving, don't hurry them either. Day sixty.

screen: `DAY 60 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A KING ON A DONKEY.`

howItsDone: Many churches read the raising of Lazarus near the end of Lent, and Orthodox Christians keep Lazarus Saturday the day before Palm Sunday. Jesus's words I am the resurrection, and the life are read at many Christian funerals.

original.note: Greek: he shed tears. A quieter word than the loud wailing of the mourners around him.

trapdoor: what you thought: jesus wept is the shortest verse, a trivia answer.
what it means: he weeps at a grave he's about to open, and stands in the grief with his friends instead of skipping past it.
what a scholar hears: John uses dakryo, quiet tears, for Jesus, and klaio, loud mourning, for Mary and the crowd, and in John this sign is what leads the authorities to plan his death.

notes: The index carry is 'jesus wept' in lowercase; kept exactly. The voice speaks it as the line.
'The shortest verse in the English Bible' — true of the KJV verse division (John 11:35); in Greek, 1 Thessalonians 5:16 is shorter. The myth game says 'King James Bible'. Confirm.
The two days' delay (John 11:6) is left as a puzzle; John frames it as for God's glory (11:4).
Dakryo (Jesus, 11:35) vs klaio (Mary and the Jews, 11:33); confirm.

The raising of Lazarus as the trigger for the plot to kill Jesus (John 11:53). Script says 'the authorities'; John 11:47 names the chief priests and Pharisees in council. Wording chosen to avoid collective blame.
Lazarus from Eleazar, 'God has helped'; Lazarus Saturday in the Orthodox calendar. Confirm.
